newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE-Flamenco star Cortes swaps gypsy caravan for jet plane.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Flamenco star Cortes swaps gypsy caravan for jet plane.

text.p: Flamenco star Joaquin Cortes, dubbed "sex on legs" for his erotic dancing and smouldering looks, has swapped the gypsy caravan for the jet plane.
He is a modern-day nomad with a mission -- to travel the world "saving" flamenco from the purists.
Like Luciano Pavarotti with opera, Cortes wants to popularise a once rarefied art and expose its swirling dances and soulful laments to a huge international audience.
The publicity machine has gone into overdrive as he takes his 30-strong troupe on a "Gypsy Passion" tour of Europe and North America.
He is treated like a rock star, his troupe is kitted out in Giorgio Armani and his liaison with supermodel Naomi Campbell gives him as much play in the gossip columns as on the arts pages.
In London to present one of the Brit pop awards alongside Campbell, Cortes was scornful of his critics.

"I don't care about the critics. I am happy to do different kinds of styles, something I have been doing since I was a child." Cortes trained with Spain's National Ballet and mixes many styles in his show.
"I am trying to popularise flamenco like Pavarotti is trying to popularise opera," said the 28-year-old son of gypsies from the Spanish city of Cordoba, his black hair tied back in a pony tail.
"I am doing a painting with my body that the audience can understand."
NOMADIC STYLE APPEALS TO CORTES

The nomadic lifestyle clearly appeals to Cortes -- another suitcase and another town is no hardship to him. "I have got this gypsy kind of spirit. I have swapped the caravan for the plane. I am a modern gypsy of the 21st century," he said.
But what about all the hype over his sex appeal as flamenco's answer to Rudolf Valentino, Casanova and Rudolf Nureyev all rolled into one?
He replies with a coy flicker of his eyelashes. "I really don't understand why I transmit that kind of sex appeal on stage. I am not trying to be sexy. We don't sell sex, we sell dance."

Cortes' bare torso glistens with sweat as he twirls in his impassioned dance routines, much to the delight of female audiences who have flocked in their thousands to watch him in London. The man is aware of the effect he has.
"I would love to go down into the audience and take a look at myself," he admits.
Michael Flatley brought recognition to Irish dancing with the acclaimed "Riverdance" show. Cortes has done the same for flamenco.
Both are relentless perfectionists who drive their troupes hard. Neither could be described as a shrinking violet.

Cortes, asked about the comparison, argues: "It will succeed if you do good work with quality and respect its tradition and roots." He also feels passionately that his dancing has stopped flamenco being "ghetto-ised." CORTES EAGER TO TRY ACTING
He likes to mix the freestyle jazz of Miles Davis with traditional flamenco music in his show. "The rhythm inside speaks the same language. Blacks and gypsies have the same roots," he said.
But Cortes is already eager to conquer new fields, and fancies acting. "I would love to be a movie actor. I am the complete artist."

A great admirer of Robert de Niro, Al Pacino, Dustin Hoffman and Jeremy Irons, he wants to play strong characters in intimate European films. "But it is very, very difficult. I would have to learn and have classes with a teacher," he said.
